subtype: Owning it quickly [Response]

subtype: Blame culture in a team [Receiver]
passage: Friday night. Today I noticed a supplier invoice had been entered twice. A small thing. But in our team, after what happened to Keerthana last month, shouted at in front of everyone over a wrong figure, nobody says anything out loud. I sat with it for two hours. Then I quietly deleted one entry and told nobody. If I reported it, I would be the next name on the whiteboard. Now the total is right, but whatever caused it is still there, and two others probably enter invoices the same way. I feel like I'm covering tracks, and I hate that. It should not feel dangerous to say "I got this wrong." - Dilnaz

qa.a: Dilnaz noticed that a supplier invoice had been entered twice.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling about quietly deleting the entry and telling nobody?
qa.a: Uneasy and ashamed, feeling like covering tracks and afraid of being blamed.

qa.q: What could the team do to make reporting mistakes safer?
qa.a: Respond to reported errors by asking what happened instead of shouting, so people can speak up.

qa.q: How did Keerthana's experience last month affect the team?
qa.a: Being shouted at in front of everyone taught the others to stay silent about problems.

grounding: Shows a worker in a punishing team hiding a small problem so it can grow unseen.

subtype: Blameless review of what happened [Response]
passage: I'm Salma, and I sat in on the review after the website went down on Saturday. I braced for names. Hemant, who led it, began differently: "We're here to understand how it unfolded. Nobody is on trial." Hemant wrote three questions on the whiteboard: What went wrong? What made that possible? What would stop it happening again? The engineer who had pushed the change spoke first, calmly, because nobody had pointed a finger. We found the update went out at five on Friday with no second reviewer on call, and the warning alert went to an inbox nobody watched. By the end we had two fixes: a second-reviewer rule and alerts sent to phones. Nobody's job was in question. I left feeling lighter.

qa.q: What three questions did Hemant write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Hemant wrote: What went wrong? What made that possible? What would stop it happening again?

qa.q: What was Salma feeling as the review began?
qa.a: Braced and worried that names would be blamed.

qa.q: What two fixes came out of the review?
qa.a: A second-reviewer rule and alerts sent to phones.

qa.q: Why did the engineer who pushed the change speak calmly?
qa.a: Nobody had pointed a finger, so it felt safe to say what happened.

grounding: Shows a team reviewing a failure by asking what happened and what conditions allowed it, fixing the system rather than the person.

subtype: Blameless review of what happened [Response]

subtype: Writing one lesson and one change [Response]
passage:
"So what's the lesson, Ramesh?" Bhupen asked, marker in hand.
"We should have tested with real data."
"True. But that's a wish. What's the concrete change?"
"Add a step to the release checklist: run the sample with last month's real file."
"Who adds it, and by when?"
"I will. Today."
Bhupen wrote on the board: Lesson: test with real data. Change: checklist item, Ramesh, today.
"And next time we look at it at the halfway point, not the end."
"Also written." Ramesh smiled. "It feels better than just saying sorry."
"Regret without a change is only regret," Bhupen said. "Let's see the checklist on Friday."

qa.q: What concrete change did Ramesh propose?
qa.a: Ramesh proposed adding a checklist step to run the sample with last month's real file.

qa.q: How does Ramesh feel by the end of the review?
qa.a: Better and relieved, since a concrete change feels better than just saying sorry.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen push past "test with real data" to a concrete change?
qa.a: A lesson without a changed action is only regret, while a named item, owner and day makes it real.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see reflection?
qa.a: Bhupen sees it as needing a changed action, not only regret.

grounding: Shows a review that ends with one lesson and one concrete change with an owner and a date.

subtype: Writing one lesson and one change [Response]

On result day I stared at the screen and thought that was it: no college, no future, everyone in the neighbourhood talking. I shut myself in my room. That same evening my uncle knocked, sat on the bed with two cups of tea and said nothing about marks. Then he said, "Tomorrow morning we'll talk to the school counsellor." We went. The counsellor listened and said that the feeling of "this is permanent" is common after a shock, and we planned the supplementary exam together. I still remember how heavy it was, and how it lifted a little.

Tea first. We'll talk about the supplementary exam later. And if this heavy feeling doesn't lift, we'll go to the school counsellor together." Rajni began to cry, and it eased a little.
